title: Focus and Deep Work
summary: Protect long blocks of attention, log distractions, practise deliberately and close each day with a shutdown ritual.
objectives: Explain attention residue and why switching tasks costs more than it seems.
Run a 50-minute focus block with a distraction log.
Use a shutdown ritual so work stops cleanly at the end of the day.

explanation.heading: Why switching is expensive
explanation.body:
When you leave one task for another, part of your attention stays behind on the first one. This is called **attention residue**. Checking a single WhatsApp message in the middle of writing a SQL query does not cost ten seconds; it can cost several minutes before your thinking is as sharp as before. A day full of small switches leaves you busy but shallow, with the feeling of having worked hard and produced little.

Deep work means giving one demanding task your full, uninterrupted attention. For a student preparing for SAP ABAP, this is the difference between reading a chapter while glancing at the phone and actually understanding internal tables well enough to write a program without notes.

explanation.heading: Focus blocks and the distraction log
explanation.body:
A **focus block** is a fixed period, usually 50 minutes, with one task, the phone out of reach, notifications off and a short break afterwards. Start with 25 minutes if 50 feels long, and add five minutes each week. Before the block write one sentence: "At the end I will have ___". A clear finish line stops drifting.

Keep a **distraction log**: a paper slip beside you. Each time the urge to check something appears, write one word (for example "cricket score", "email", "reel") and return to work. The log does two things. It lets the urge pass without acting, and at the end of the week it shows your real triggers. Most people discover two or three repeating ones, and those can be removed at the source: phone in another room, site blockers, or a set time to check messages.

explanation.heading: Deliberate practice
explanation.body:
Time spent is not the same as skill gained. **Deliberate practice** means working at the edge of your ability with a specific target, immediate feedback and repetition of the weak part. Re-reading notes feels productive but is easy. Writing an ABAP loop from memory, checking it against the answer and redoing the line you got wrong is hard and effective.

Use four steps: choose one small skill, attempt it without help, check the result against a correct version, then repeat only the part that failed. Thirty minutes of this beats two hours of passive review.

explanation.heading: The shutdown ritual
explanation.body: Unfinished tasks keep nagging at the mind in the evening. A **shutdown ritual** is a short fixed routine, five minutes at most, that tells your brain the day is closed. Review what is done, write tomorrow's top three tasks, note any loose thread in one line, tidy your desk and say a closing phrase such as "Done for today". Because the plan exists on paper, your mind can rest, and tomorrow starts without a decision about where to begin.

examples.title: A real focus block
examples.body: Aman sets a 50-minute timer, leaves his phone in the next room and writes: "At the end I will have solved six SQL join problems." He logs three urges: "reel", "email", "tea". After the block he sees "reel" appears daily at the same time, so he moves his phone charger outside his study room.
examples.takeaway: The log turns urges into data you can act on.

examples.title: Deliberate versus passive
examples.body: Priya reads a chapter on data types twice and feels confident. Her friend writes ten declarations from memory, compares them with the book, finds three errors and repeats those three. The friend learns more in 30 minutes.
examples.takeaway: Attempt, check, repeat the weak part.

exercises.modelAnswer: Task: solve six SQL join problems. Finish: "At the end I will have six solved queries and notes on two errors." Length: 50 minutes. Phone in my bag in the other room, notifications off. I will keep a paper slip and write one word per urge, then review the slip on Sunday and remove the most frequent trigger.
exercises.guidance: Strong plans have one task, a finish line that you can check, a phone out of reach and a plan to review the log. Avoid listing three tasks in one block.

quiz.prompt: Checking messages during a coding task mainly costs you:
quiz.why: Residue from the switch slows full focus for minutes.

quiz.prompt: What is the purpose of the distraction log?
options: To let urges pass and reveal repeating triggers
quiz.why: Logging lets you resist the urge and shows triggers to remove.

quiz.prompt: Which element is essential to deliberate practice?
options: Feedback and repeating the weak part
quiz.why: Feedback on a specific weak point is what drives improvement.

quiz.prompt: The shutdown ritual lasts at most ____ minutes. (one word)
quiz.why: It is short, five minutes at most, so you will actually do it.

bank.prompt: To reduce attention residue you should:
options: Finish or park a task cleanly before switching
bank.why: Parking a task with a note frees attention for the next.

options: One task, one finish line and phone away
bank.why: One clear task and fewer distractions make it work.

options: So your mind can rest and tomorrow starts fast
bank.why: A written plan closes open loops in the mind.
